content: Naegleria is a free-living amoeba that is commonly found in the environment, particularly in water and soil. While human infections are rare, they are extremely serious. To reduce the risk of infection, it is important to take precautions to prevent water from entering the nose during recreational water activities. Only one species of Naegleria, known as Naegleria fowleri, is capable of infecting humans. Although infection with Naegleria fowleri is very rare, it is most likely to occur during the dry, hot summer months when air temperatures are high, water is warm, and water levels are low. The incidence of infections tends to increase during years with heat waves. Once symptoms of infection begin, the disease progresses rapidly and is typically fatal within approximately five days, though the range can vary from one to twelve days. Naegleria fowleri causes a condition known as primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), a severe brain infection that leads to the destruction of brain tissue. In its early stages, the symptoms of PAM may resemble those of bacterial meningitis. Initial symptoms usually appear about five days after infection, with a range of one to seven days. These early symptoms may include headache, fever, nausea, and vomiting. As the disease progresses, later symptoms can include a stiff neck, confusion, lack of attention to people and surroundings, loss of balance, seizures, and hallucinations. The diagnosis of Naegleria fowleri infection can be made through microscopic examination of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). A wet mount may reveal motile trophozoites, while a Giemsa-stained smear can show trophozoites with characteristic morphology. Additional diagnostic methods, such as confocal microscopy, cultivation of the organism, and identification using direct immunofluorescent antibody techniques, may also be helpful. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based techniques, both conventional and real-time, have been increasingly used to detect and identify free-living amoebic infections in clinical samples. These advanced diagnostic methods are typically available in specialized reference laboratories. Several drugs have demonstrated effectiveness against Naegleria fowleri in laboratory settings. However, their clinical efficacy remains uncertain, as nearly all infections have been fatal even with treatment. Amphotericin B has been successfully used in some cases to treat PAM caused by Naegleria fowleri.
